paragraphs.heading: A shell from a dying star
paragraphs.text: A planetary nebula is a glowing, expanding shell of ionized gas that a red giant star throws off late in its life. Despite the name, it has nothing to do with planets: through early telescopes these objects looked round, like planets. Every one of them forms as a star of intermediate mass reaches its end, about 1 to 8 times the Sun's, and the Sun is expected to make one too. Spectra show that every planetary nebula is expanding.

paragraphs.heading: How it glows
paragraphs.text: Once all of the red giant's atmosphere has drifted away, its hot, luminous core is left bare. This core, called the planetary nebula nucleus, gives off strong ultraviolet light that ionizes the gas thrown off earlier. The gas absorbs that light and is energized, which makes the shell shine in bright colours. By the standards of a star's life the display is brief, lasting perhaps a few tens of thousands of years.

paragraphs.heading: Why they matter
paragraphs.text: Planetary nebulae probably play a key part in the chemical evolution of the Milky Way, carrying elements out of the stars that made them and into the space between stars. They are seen in more distant galaxies too, where they give useful clues about those galaxies' chemical make-up. Starting in the 1990s, Hubble Space Telescope images showed that many have very complex and varied shapes. Only about a fifth are roughly round. Why they take so many forms is still not well understood, though binary central stars, stellar winds and magnetic fields may be involved.

paragraphs.heading: Named for a look-alike
paragraphs.text: The first one found was the Dumbbell Nebula in the constellation Vulpecula, which Charles Messier observed on July 12, 1764, and listed as M27. To early observers with low-resolution telescopes, it and later finds looked like giant planets such as Uranus. In 1779 Antoine Darquier de Pellepoix described the Ring Nebula as being as large as Jupiter and looking like a fading planet. William Herschel, who in the 1780s also likened them to planets, used the name "planetary nebulae"; where the term came from is unknown, but astronomers still use it today.

paragraphs.heading: A line no one could explain
paragraphs.text: What these objects were stayed a mystery until the first spectra were taken in the mid-19th century. William Huggins spread their light out with a prism, and on August 29, 1864, he became the first to analyse the spectrum of a planetary nebula, the Cat's Eye Nebula. Stars had shown him a continuous spread of light crossed by many dark lines, but the Cat's Eye showed a number of bright emission lines instead. The brightest, at 500.7 nanometres, matched no known element. Some proposed a new element, named nebulium, much as helium had been found in the Sun's spectrum in 1868, but unlike helium, nebulium was never isolated on Earth.

paragraphs.heading: Forbidden lines
paragraphs.text: In the early 20th century Henry Norris Russell suggested the 500.7 nm line came from a familiar element in unfamiliar conditions. In the 1920s physicists showed that in gas of extremely low density, electrons can sit in excited levels that collisions would empty in denser gas. Electrons leaving these levels in ions of nitrogen and oxygen produce the 500.7 nm line and others. These lines, seen only in very low-density gas, are called forbidden lines, and they showed that the nebulae are made of extremely thin gas.
